steps.observation: You have 300 seconds. Write a short story about a lighthouse keeper.

steps.action:
Gulls wheeled through the salt-sharp air as Elias Harlan lit the lighthouse lamp for the night. Forty years he had tended Grayhook Light, a granite finger planted on a ragged cliff above the North Atlantic. In all that time storms had gnawed the coast, ships had come and gone, and the world beyond the waves had hurried along without him. Yet every dusk Elias performed the same quiet ritual: polish the Fresnel lens, trim the wick, strike the match, and let the beacon bloom like a second sun.

Tonight, though, the ocean felt different. The wind arrived in strange bursts, blowing warm then cold, like two seasons wrestling. Low on the horizon a bruised line of clouds rolled toward Grayhook, flashing pale, silent lightning. Elias watched, uneasy. He’d read the weather nearly all his life, but this storm carried a mood he couldn’t name.

He wound the clockwork mechanism that rotated the lamp, its gears whispering like old secrets. Then he climbed onto the balcony, looking down at the village—tiny, sleepy windows winking yellow—before turning his eyes back to the creeping dark. The radio on his belt crackled. “Harbor patrol to Grayhook. Elias, you seeing this?”

“Aye,” he answered. “Looks like trouble.”

“Fishing trawler Marigold still at sea. Last position ten miles out, heading in blind. We’ve lost radar.”

Elias felt the words settle like stones in his chest. The Marigold’s captain was Nora Finch, a woman who had grown up borrowing his spyglass to watch whales. He pictured her stubborn grin, her hair whipped by the ever-present wind.

“Copy,” he said. “I’ll keep the beam true.”

The storm struck suddenly, smashing waves against the cliff. Rain lashed sideways, turning the beacon’s glow into spinning white veils. Power flickered, then failed—the bulb died, and the tower plunged into blackness. Somewhere beyond the roar, a ship’s horn bellowed, frightened.

Heart hammering, Elias dashed down two spiral flights to the workshop. He yanked open a dusty crate marked ACETYLENE—EMERGENCY FLARE LAMP, last used decades ago. Hands trembling, he assembled the antique tripod on the balcony, fed the gas, struck a spark. A wild orange flame burst forth, nothing like the steady electric beam but fierce, defiant.

He hauled the contraption to the lantern room, aimed it seaward, and opened the shutters. The flame painted the storm in molten streaks, a primal fire calling across centuries. Thunder answered, but somewhere in the blur of rain he glimpsed a shape: the Marigold’s mast, tilting, then righting itself as the vessel steered toward the lee side of the headland.

Minutes crawled. At last a distant horn blew twice in gratitude. Elias exhaled for the first time in what felt like hours.

Dawn peeled the clouds apart, laying soft gold on everything bruised and broken. The power returned with a hum; the electric bulb rekindled, tame compared to the night’s savage blaze. Down in the harbor, the Marigold sat safely moored. Nora herself climbed the cliff path, carrying a thermos of coffee and a grin wider than the horizon.

“Old man,” she called up, “your fire could’ve lit the whole ocean.”

Elias smiled, shoulders aching, eyes red. “That’s the idea,” he replied.

And as the sunrise ignited the sky, Grayhook Light kept shining—because a keeper’s duty was never simply to guard a lamp, but to refuse the darkness its victory, night after night.
